subject: biology
title: Enzymes Adventure 2 · Calculations
welcome_lead: How temperature, pH and substrate change enzyme rates.
meta_desc: GCSE Biology Enzymes — effect of temperature, pH (pepsin pH 2, amylase pH 7) and substrate concentration on enzyme rate.
final_note: You can describe how temperature, pH and substrate concentration change enzyme rate, and you know pepsin's optimum is pH 2, salivary amylase pH 7, and intestinal enzymes around pH 8.

concepts.def: Temperature or pH where the enzyme works fastest
Active site changed shape — substrate no longer fits
Amount of substrate per unit volume

walkthroughs.body_html:
As temperature rises, enzymes and substrates move faster and collide more often → rate goes up.

But past the optimum (about 37 °C for human enzymes), the enzyme's shape starts to break.

The active site changes shape — the substrate no longer fits — and the enzyme is denatured. Rate crashes to zero.

Each enzyme has its own optimum pH. Move away from it and the active site changes shape → denaturation.

- Pepsin (stomach protease): optimum pH 2 — the stomach is very acidic.
- Salivary amylase (mouth): optimum pH 7 — neutral saliva.
- Trypsin / intestinal lipase: optimum pH ~8 — bile makes the small intestine slightly alkaline.

Add more substrate → more collisions with active sites → rate rises.

But eventually every active site is busy. Adding more substrate makes no difference — the rate plateaus.

To make it rise further, you'd need to add more enzyme.

mcqs.q: What is the optimum pH of pepsin in the stomach?
options: pH 2
pH 5
pH 7
pH 9

mcqs.q: What happens to an enzyme past its optimum temperature?
options: It speeds up forever
It denatures and stops working
It becomes a substrate
Nothing changes

mcqs.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: The enzyme has died because enzymes are alive.
The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
Its tertiary structure (3D shape) changes, particularly the active site, so it can no longer bind substrate effectively.
Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.

mcqs.q: Why are enzymes specific to certain substrates?
options: Each enzyme can react with any substrate, but works fastest with one type.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
Only substrates with complementary shape and chemistry to the active site can bind effectively.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
options: Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
Both move substances down a concentration gradient, but active transport is faster.
Active transport requires energy (ATP) and can move substances against the concentration gradient.
